papers.title: IntentGR: Enhancing Intent for End-to-End Personalized Generative Retrieval in Search
papers.en: IntentGR: Enhancing Intent for End-to-End Personalized Generative Retrieval in Search
papers.authors: Gefan Ye, Yanjing Wu, Yinfu Feng, Zhiqiang Wang, Liang Li, Jun Xiao
papers.abstract: Personalized generative retrieval in search should jointly satisfy the user's immediate search intent and long-term preference. Recent end-to-end approaches, primarily explored in recommendation, unify item tokenization and sequence generation within a single model, allowing semantic identifiers (SIDs) to be optimized toward the downstream generation objective. However, these methods often treat the query merely as an input feature, without explicitly leveraging it to guide either identifier learning or sequence generation. This leaves intent guidance weak in both the tokenization and the generation stage, causing generated semantic identifiers to drift toward high-frequency token patterns rather than the current search intent. In this work, we find that incorporating additional query-related evidence into the framework of end-to-end generative retrieval is important. Based on this finding, we propose IntentGR, an intent-enhanced end-to-end framework that strengthens query semantics at four complementary stages of the retrieval pipeline. Query-Aware Semantic Behavior Representation (QBR) introduces query-level behavioral evidence as a new input signal; Query-Semantic Alignment (QSA), Long-Tail Query Enrichment (LQE), and Query-conditioned Attention Modulation (QAM) then serve as integration mechanisms at the optimization, training-distribution, and decoding stages to fully exploit this evidence. Experiments on the public AOL4PS benchmark and AE, a large-scale industrial e-commerce dataset, show that IntentGR improves Recall@10 by 8.11% and 11.96% over the strongest baseline, with strong gains on long-tail queries. These results suggest that enriched query-related input evidence, together with effective integration mechanisms, is beneficial for building intent-aware end-to-end generative search systems.

papers.title: How Developer Personality Shapes the Use of AI Coding Assistants
papers.en: How Developer Personality Shapes the Use of AI Coding Assistants
papers.authors: Annemarie Wittig, Alina Mailach, Norbert Siegmund
papers.abstract: Developers differ in personality traits that shape how they approach software development tasks, yet AI coding assistants either behave uniformly or offer personalization features whose fit with individual developers must be found through trial and error. This is because it remains unclear how personality shapes developers' experiences with AI assistants, and thus which traits personalization should account for. In other words, we provide tools with no underlying theory on what works when and why. We take a first step towards such a theory with a systematic scoping review on how users' personality relates to their perception of LLM-based tools. We identified twelve studies through general search engines, major Software Engineering (SE) venues, AI tooling, and snowballing. They all reported associations between personality and perceptions, particularly perceived usefulness, yet none addressed this in a SE context. Building on these findings, we conducted an exploratory two-wave survey with 29 and 11 developers, collecting first empirical evidence of how developers' personality (measured using the Big Five Model) relates to the perception of AI coding assistants. Higher Extraversion was associated with more positive private-use experiences in both waves, while Agreeableness was associated with negative professional experiences in the first wave and positive ones in the second. These results provide first indications that the personality effects found in the literature extend to developers. Although further studies with bigger samples are needed to build a theory, our work takes the first step towards an empirical grounded theory of developer personality and AI personalization traits.

papers.title: User First Intelligence: Three Measurements of Search and AI-Answer Analytics (SEO and GEO/AEO), and a Knowledge-Graph Framework for Query Discovery Beyond Search Volume
papers.en: User First Intelligence: Three Measurements of Search and AI-Answer Analytics (SEO and GEO/AEO), and a Knowledge-Graph Framework for Query Discovery Beyond Search Volume
papers.abstract: People say what they want to know in many places besides a search box, and the tools that search and AI-answer optimization (SEO and GEO/AEO) rely on see only part of that demand, through models reported as counts. This paper reports three measurements of such instruments and a framework. On the area-code section of a large US telecom provider's site, two commercial analytics platforms differed on estimated monthly visits by 7.5x to 27.1x (8.6x to 29.9x worldwide); across twelve sections of the domain the ratio ran from 0.20x to 7.24x with no detectable relation to section age, while they agreed on which section is larger in 60 of 66 pairs. On 37,193 reviews of 378 telecom stores linked to a 42,994-node keyword taxonomy, review demand and search volume agreed on branches to a varying degree (Spearman 0.47 to 0.75; 0.91 post hoc) and barely on topics (0.18), on links two blind AI annotators judged two-thirds correct; on the 372 area codes, a public count of Wikipedia requests for each code and vendor volume agreed roughly on ranking (0.45 over 240 articles, gone once keywords matched per code are held constant) and not on magnitudes, predictions fixed first. In one vendor's index of AI answers naming or citing the largest companies of each S&P 500 sector, of four predictions written first, one held, one in direction only and two failed; video and community sites took a median 21% of citation incidences on Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode against 0.6% to 9.2% on four other surfaces, in every sector, and in education answers in each of 13 countries read later. Estimates and sources need measuring per instrument and surface. User First Intelligence (UFI), built on that premise, collects what people ask beyond the website, links it to an industry ontology and scores where an organization does not answer; an open implementation is released, its score not evaluated. No causal claim is made.

papers.title: AI-Mediated Communication Can Steer Collective Opinion
papers.en: AI-Mediated Communication Can Steer Collective Opinion
papers.authors: Stratis Tsirtsis, Kaivalya Rawal, Chris Russell, Brent Mittelstadt, Sandra Wachter
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into the online platforms where humans exchange opinions; large language models (LLMs) have been polishing users' posts on LinkedIn and providing context for content shared on X. While prior work has shown that AI can express biased opinions and shape individuals' opinions during human-AI interactions, less attention has been paid to its influence on collective opinion formation when mediating human-to-human communication. We address this gap via a combination of empirical and theoretical analyses. We show empirically that LLMs from multiple popular families introduce directional biases when instructed to edit human-written texts on contested topics, for example, nudging texts in favor of gun control and against atheism. Building on this observation, we introduce a mathematical model of opinion dynamics in which an AI system sits between users on a social network, transforming the opinions they express and perceive. By analytically characterizing the equilibrium of this model and performing simulations on real social network data, we show that biases introduced by AI in human-to-human communication can be amplified through the network and shift collective opinion in their direction. In light of these findings, we investigate whether such biases are controllable by online platforms. We audit the "Explain this post" feature on X and find evidence of pro-life bias in Grok's outputs on abortion-related content, which we trace back to specific design choices. We conclude with a discussion of the broader implications of our findings in relation to ongoing legislative efforts in the European Union.
